justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored to what I assumed was the current market price of the underlying asset, likely a major equity index ETF or similar instrument trading around 420–425. For the one-day horizon, I set the estimate at 424, reflecting a modest drift assumption consistent with recent momentum and the tendency for markets to exhibit slight positive bias over very short periods when no major catalysts are imminent. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the figure slightly higher to 426, acknowledging that weekly returns on equity instruments have historically averaged small positive values, though this marginal optimism is tempered by mean-reversion tendencies. The one-month estimate of 430 extends that gentle upward drift further, consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations but deliberately restrained given the many things that can shift over a 30-day window.

The confidence interval widths reflect standard realized volatility scaling across time horizons. For a single day, historical daily volatility on instruments in this price range typically runs around 1–1.5%, which translates to a range of roughly plus or minus 14 points at the 90% level, giving the 410–438 band. For one week, volatility scales by roughly the square root of five, widening the interval to about plus or minus 26 points, producing the 400–452 range. The one-month interval widens further to plus or minus 50 points, capturing the compounding uncertainty over approximately 21 trading days. These widths also implicitly allow for some fat-tail behavior, since equity returns are known to be leptokurtic, meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a pure normal distribution would suggest.

Several risks could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a surprise spike in unemployment claims, a worse-than-expected inflation print, or a credit event in a systemically important institution — could trigger a rapid selloff exceeding the lower bounds I specified. Geopolitical shocks, including escalation in active conflict zones or unexpected sanctions announcements, represent another tail risk. On the upside, a dovish pivot from a major central bank, a breakthrough in trade negotiations, or a blowout earnings season could push prices through the upper bounds. For the one-month horizon in particular, the interval could be violated by any accumulation of sequential surprises in either direction, since compounding sentiment shifts over weeks can produce moves far larger than volatility models trained on quieter periods would anticipate.
